manual.title: User manual
manual.intro: How the platform is worked, from the first sign-in to the last guest. Each chapter reads in a minute.

signIn.title: Signing in
steps: The end client and the staff sign in without a password: you type your email at /entrar and a six-digit code arrives.
The platform account and office administrators may also have a password, to get in on the days the mail is not moving. The link sits under the code field.
The code works ONCE and expires after ten minutes. If it runs out, ask for another.
The answer is the same whether the account exists or not: the system never reveals who is registered.
You sign out from your account menu, at the end of the header. On a shared computer, always sign out.

interface.title: Your account menu
steps: At the end of the header is your photo with your name. Everything of yours lives in there: who you are, which office and role you are working with, “My profile”, the language and “Sign out”.
They are together on purpose: they are things about WHOEVER is signed in, not about the site. And “Sign out” is no longer loose beside the navigation links, where it got clicked by accident.
The language is saved on YOUR account, not the office’s: two colleagues at the same desk can read it in different languages.
Choosing Arabic turns the whole panel right to left, not just the words.
This does not touch the invitations’ language: that is decided per version, on the event’s page.
On a phone only the photo is left, without the name: the header has no room for both.

profile.title: My profile
steps: “My profile” is yours and yours alone: your name, photo, phone, the language you read the panel in, the country you handle and your timezone. The email is not changed here: it is what you sign in with.
Changing it changes nothing for the rest of the office. Two people at the same counter can work in different languages.

The photo is UPLOADED from your phone or computer; there is no address to paste. The server crops it to a square, shrinks it and strips what phone photos carry inside — the place it was taken among it. To remove it, tick “Remove the photo on save”.

The country is not decoration: it decides the dialling code a pasted guest list without one is normalised to, and a new event’s timezone. Working from Costa Rica? Set it and stop typing +506 every time.
The timezone decides which clock YOU read the panel’s times by. Leaving it empty means the one of the country you handle.
Only the platform account and office administrators have a password; everyone else signs in with the emailed code. Changing it closes every other session, which is exactly what it is changed for.

At the bottom is “Where you are signed in”: every device the account was opened from, with the last time and the address. A session lasts thirty days, so if you left one open on somebody else’s computer, close it there.
The role is NOT here, deliberately: nobody promotes themselves. That is changed by whoever administers, under “Team”.

create.title: Creating an invitation
steps: /crear has six steps: language and event type, names, when and where, details, other languages, and review.
The preview on the side is the real invitation — the same component the guest will see. What you see is what gets published.
The event type decides the template and the colours. A memorial never uses the celebration template, and the form cannot force it.
The verse is chosen from a closed, verified list. There is no free-text field for a sacred text, deliberately.
Publishing needs a session and uses one event of your plan. The limit is checked on the server as you publish.

languages.title: The languages
steps: The language you pick in step 1 is the main one: the invitation is created in it, and it is the fallback.
In step 5 you can write the same invitation in the other languages. You write the text: nothing is translated for you.
The names, the date and the venue are the same in every version. Only the message and the verse change.
Each version has its own writing direction, its own numerals and its own public link.
You can also add a language later, from the event's page.
Each guest opens the version in THEIR language. Anyone without one gets the main version, and the guest list flags it in red.

guests.title: The guest list
steps: On the event's page you paste the list or upload a file. One line per guest: name, phone, language.
Commas, semicolons and tabs all work. If the first line is headers, it is detected on its own.
Pick the country code before importing: phone numbers are stored in international format.
A line with no name is skipped and counted. An empty guest is never imported.
Pasting the same list again duplicates nobody: guests are matched by phone, and by name when there is no phone.

send.title: Sending over WhatsApp
steps: Each guest has their own link, short and without the event's name, so forwarding it does not reveal whose wedding it is.
The button opens YOUR WhatsApp with the message already written. It goes out from your number, the one your clients know.
The message is in the guest's language, not the office's.
There is no per-message fee and no templates to get approved: this is not the WhatsApp API, it is your own WhatsApp.
A guest with no phone shows a link to copy and send however you like.
If pasting the links one by one gets long, you can connect your own number by QR code and let them go out gradually. That is the next chapter, and the warning there is worth reading first.
Once a number is connected, the “Send by WhatsApp” section on the event screen queues the whole batch. The button does NOT send: it writes rows, and the sender is the service with its brake.

The “Send on” field decides WHEN. Empty means now. With a date, the batch waits and goes out on its own that day even if nobody signs in: a wedding is announced on the day the couple chose, not the day you sat down with the list.

The time is on YOUR clock, not the server’s. If you work from Costa Rica and the wedding is in Beirut, write the time you want it to go out and the system converts it. The timezone comes from your profile.
While it waits, the screen says so and there is a button to cancel it. What already went out cannot be cancelled: it is on somebody’s phone.
Below, “Remind whoever has not replied”: pick how many days before the wedding and that is all. The system checks by itself every fifteen minutes and queues the reminder when it is due.
That reminder goes ONLY to those who have not replied and have a phone, once, in their own language. Whoever already said yes or no is not written to again, and after the wedding nothing is sent.

whatsappQr.title: Connecting a WhatsApp number
steps: This is for not pasting two hundred links by hand. It does NOT replace sending one by one: that stays in the guest table and is what always works.
Before anything, read the red warning on the screen. Automating a personal number goes against WhatsApp's terms, and the number they can close is yours.
Under Settings › WhatsApp: give the number a name (“Hamra counter”) and press Add.
On the row that appears, press Connect. The code takes a few seconds and the screen refreshes by itself.
Scan it from the phone: WhatsApp › Settings › Linked devices › Link a device. Same gesture as WhatsApp Web.
The session is stored encrypted, so there is no rescanning every time the server restarts.
You can connect several numbers, one per counter. Mark the default one on its row.
Start with few messages and raise it slowly, over weeks not hours. The daily cap is on each number's row.

packages.title: Selling packages and getting paid
steps: The wedding's screen has “Sell a package”: 100, 200 or 500 invitations. The price is not typed in; it comes from the event's channel.
Enter the couple's name and WhatsApp, pick the package, and create. A payment link comes out.
That link goes out on WhatsApp with a button. The couple opens it WITHOUT an account, sees it in their own language, and pays on Whish's page.
Invitations unlock when Whish confirms the payment, not before. A pending order unlocks nothing.
For cash, switch it on under Settings › Payments and mark it yourself from the package's row. It goes into the history with your name.
Packages add up: a wedding that grows buys another one without giving the first back.
Until the event has a paid package, the guest limit is the office's plan.

rsvp.title: Replies
steps: The guest answers on the invitation page itself, with no account and no password.
Opening the link records the date, so you can see who received it even before they answer.
The event's page sums up who is coming, who is not, and how many they bring.
The download button hands you the list as CSV with a byte-order mark, so Excel does not wreck the Arabic.
Every invitation has a calendar file, so the guest can save it to their phone.

tables.title: The seating plan
steps: Reached from the event, under “Seating plan”, next to the guest list.
Create the tables with a name and how many seats. Leave the name empty and they come out as “Table 1”, “Table 2”…
Only guests who said YES are seated. Someone who never replied takes no chair, and someone who replied for four takes four.
“Seat the ones left” fills the tables in order without splitting a group. Move anybody afterwards with their own dropdown.
If somebody is seated and later says they are not coming, nobody clears them automatically: they stay flagged at their table and a person decides.
Two lists print: by table, for the venue and the caterer; and by guest in alphabetical order, for whoever is at the door.
The guest sees their table on their own personal link — the one already on their phone.

image.title: The image
steps: Each invitation is rendered as a 1080×1920 PNG on the server, with the same layout as the page.
The image is stored the first time and reused. It is also the preview WhatsApp asks for when the link is shared.
Adding ?download=1 to the end of the image address downloads it instead of opening it.
If anything on the invitation changes, a new image is made on its own: the fingerprint covers everything that changes the drawing.

team.title: The office's team
steps: Each office sees only its own events. One office never reaches another's data.
There are four roles: superadmin, office admin, operator and organiser.
The operator creates and edits events and guests. The organiser only looks.
Billing and the team are managed by the office admin.
Permissions are always checked on the server: a button you cannot see is not a permission.

roles.title: Roles and permissions
steps: Each role holds a list of permissions, and Settings › Roles and permissions spells out in full what each one grants.
The system's owner can adjust what each role may do, and go back to the defaults at any time.
Two things are never touched: the superadmin entirely, and the platform-administration permission. If that one could be handed out, anyone would grant it to their own role.
Changing a person's role happens under “Team”, row by row.
Permissions are checked on the server. A hidden button is not a permission: not seeing and not being able are different things, and here they are both.

config.title: The system's settings
steps: The system's owner only. Seven sections: Mail, Payments, WhatsApp, Roles and permissions, Brand, Home page and The site.
Each field says where its value comes from: saved here, inherited from the server, or not set. And it carries what to write and where to get it.
Saving one section does not touch the others.
Mail: without this, nobody can sign in with a code. There is a button that sends a test email and shows the provider's answer.
Payments: Whish, cash and — once there are credentials — SINPE Móvil are switched on separately. The test button reads the balance, so it checks the credentials without moving money.

Brand: the system’s name, and the logo and tab icon, which are UPLOADED from your computer — no address to paste. There is a preview on a dark background, which is where the logo will live. The logo keeps its shape; the icon is cropped to a square, because a tab is one.
Home page: every text on the front page, in all four languages. An empty field uses the original text.
Passwords are stored encrypted and the screen never gives them back: they are replaced, not read. An empty field means “leave it alone”.

system.title: System status
steps: Only the superadmin sees it, because it names the configuration variables that are missing.
At the top, eleven checks: database, outgoing mail, payment gateway, encryption key, Chromium and the rest. Green is fine; red says exactly what is missing.
Below, the versions of everything running, read live from the machine.
The "Send a test email" button sends a real message to the superadmin and shows the server’s answer. It is the only thing that tells "misconfigured" apart from "the provider refuses the password".
The server accepting the message does not guarantee it reaches the inbox. If it does not turn up, check the spam folder before touching anything.
Updating packages is done from the console, not from there: the screen gives the exact commands.

system.title: System status
system.intro: What this installation is running, and whether anything is missing for it to work. The figures are read live, not typed in by hand.

hints.PAYMENTS_PROVIDER: Type “whish” to charge for real. Anything else does not charge, and in production the code refuses to start with the test one.
hints.WHISH_CHANNEL: Whish gives you this with the MERCHANT ACCOUNT. It is not in the personal app: ask for it at Whish Business.
hints.WHISH_WEBSITE_URL: The domain you registered with Whish, without https://. Here: citas.posxml.com
hints.WHISH_SECRET: Also given by Whish with the merchant account. It is not your app password.
hints.MAILER: Type “smtp” to send for real. Anything else only prints to the log.
hints.MAIL_FROM: It is called MAIL_FROM, not SMTP_FROM. Format: Your Brand <info@your-domain.com>
hints.CONTACT_WHATSAPP: In E.164 without the plus: 96170123456. Empty = it does not appear on the home page.
hints.HOME_SECTIONS: Comma-separated, in this order: features, steps, showcase, pricing, faq, closing. Remove one to hide it.
hints.WHATSAPP_GATEWAY_URL: Where the WhatsApp service listens. Defaults to http://127.0.0.1:4100, and must not be published.
hints.WHATSAPP_DELAY_MIN: Between 3 and 300. The real delay is random between minimum and maximum: an exact interval is a machine's signature. It cannot be zero — the brake can be shortened, not removed.
hints.WHATSAPP_DELAY_MAX: Between 3 and 600. If it falls below the minimum, the minimum is used.
hints.WHATSAPP_WARMUP_CAP: Between 1 and 100. A newly connected number sends this on its first day, even if its daily cap is higher. Raise it slowly: over weeks, not hours.

whatsapp.hint: Each number connects by scanning a code from the phone, just like WhatsApp Web. The session is stored encrypted, so there is no rescanning after a restart.

features.heading: Everything it takes to invite
features.subheading: No generic templates and no machine translation.

languages.title: Four real languages
languages.body: Arabic, Spanish, Portuguese and English. Arabic runs right to left across the whole card, with its own numerals and its own typeface. Each guest opens the version in their own language.

whatsapp.title: Sent over WhatsApp
whatsapp.body: Every guest gets their own link from the number their family already knows. No approved templates and no per-message fee.

rsvp.title: Replies that count themselves
rsvp.body: Guests answer on the same page, with no account and no password. You see who opened it, who is coming and how many they bring.

tables.title: The room laid out
tables.body: Who sits at which table, counting the companions on every reply. Prints by table for the venue and by guest for the door, and each guest sees their table on the link already on their phone.

image.title: An image ready to share
image.body: The same invitation comes out as a 1080×1920 PNG rendered on the server. Download it, print it, or send it as it is.

verses.title: Verses checked by a person
verses.body: Qur'anic and biblical texts come from a fixed list a human has verified. A machine never writes them.

offices.title: Built for offices
offices.body: Each office sees only its own events, with its own team, plan and invoices. An event never crosses from one office to another.

steps.heading: Three steps

write.title: Write it

send.title: Send it

track.title: Follow it

showcase.heading: Two templates, two tones

pricing.heading: Pricing
pricing.subheading: One event, or a whole office.

guestApp.question: Does the guest have to install anything?
guestApp.answer: No. The invitation is a web link that opens in the phone's browser. No account, no password and no app.

languages.question: Do you translate the invitation?
languages.answer: Not automatically, and that is deliberate. You write the text for each language; we never transliterate a family name or paraphrase a verse. The names, the date and the venue are shared by every version.

payment.question: How is payment taken in Lebanon?
payment.answer: Through Whish. Payment is confirmed server to server: coming back to the success page is never proof that anything was paid.

print.question: Can I print it?
print.answer: Yes. Every invitation downloads as a 1080×1920 PNG rendered on the server — the same one the guest sees.

ownNumber.question: Do the messages come from my number?
ownNumber.answer: Yes. We open your own WhatsApp with the message already written, so it goes out from the number your clients already know.

closing.heading: Is there a wedding this season?
closing.body: Write the invitation, paste the list and send it today.

footer.tagline: Digital invitations in Arabic, Spanish, Portuguese and English.

share.whatsappMessage: Hello {name}, we would love to have you with us. Here is the invitation: {link}
share.reminderMessage: Hello {name}, we are still hoping to hear from you and it would mean a lot to have you there. Here is the invitation: {link}

pay.heading: Your invitation package
pay.hosted: Payment happens on Whish's own page. Nothing about your card or account is asked for here.
pay.paidBody: Thank you. Your package is active and the office can send the invitations.
pay.pendingTitle: We have no record of the payment yet
pay.pendingBody: If you have just paid, wait a moment and check again.
pay.failedTitle: The payment did not go through
pay.failedBody: You have not been charged. You can try again.
pay.providerError: The payment page could not be opened. Try again in a few minutes, or tell the office.
pay.notFound: This link does not exist, or is no longer available.
pay.cashDefault: You can pay at the office. As soon as we record it, your invitations are unlocked.
pay.orNothing: No payment method is configured yet. Please tell the office.
